title: Pediatric Toxic Ingestion — "One Pill Can Kill"
keywords: a history of a single missing pill or a small unknown taste is enough to trigger a real workup in a toddler for this specific list of agents, do not wait for symptoms to develop before taking it seriously

sulfonylureas, calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers, opioids, TCAs, and clonidine already have their own management references in this app, this module is the peds-specific triage layer that routes to them
camphor causes seizures fast, often within 5-90 minutes, and there is no antidote, management is supportive and seizure control
methyl salicylate — oil of wintergreen — is concentrated enough that under a teaspoon has killed a toddler, treat it as aspirin overdose but with a much smaller lethal volume
chloroquine and other antimalarials cause rapid cardiac dysfunction and seizures, a single adult tablet can be lethal to a small child
sources: Michael JB, Sztajnkrycer MD. Deadly pediatric poisons: nine common agents that kill at low doses. Emerg Med Clin North Am. 2004;22(4):1019-1050.
Matteucci MJ. One pill can kill: assessing the potential for fatal poisonings in children. Pediatr Ann. 2005;34(12):964-968.
Bar-Oz B, et al. Medications that can be fatal for a toddler with one tablet or teaspoonful ingestion. Drug Saf. 2004;27(14):1057-1082.

changelog.change: Initial entry — a genuine content gap (Content audit 2026-09-15, fresh-look Batch 6). Deliberately scoped to avoid duplicating existing adult toxicology reference content — cardiovascular agents (CCB, beta-blocker, clonidine), TCAs, opioids, and sulfonylureas already have management detail elsewhere in the corpus; this module supplies the missing pediatric-specific triage framing plus standalone content for the genuinely uncovered agents (camphor, methyl salicylate, chloroquine/antimalarials).
Reformatted for reading on a phone: long paragraphs broken into short paragraphs and lists. Wording and clinical content unchanged.

purpose: Recognize which common household medications are potentially lethal to a toddler from a single dose, and route to the right management reference — the exposure history alone (even 'just one pill, found the bottle open') should trigger a real workup for this specific list.
ageRange: Toddlers/young children, roughly under 6 years old and under ~10 kg is the classic highest-risk weight range — the same absolute dose is proportionally far more dangerous than in an older child or adult.

body.text: For this specific list of agents, a history of a single missing pill, an open bottle, or even a small unknown taste is enough to warrant a real evaluation — do NOT wait for the child to become symptomatic before taking the exposure seriously. Many of these agents have delayed or deceptively brief early symptoms before a life-threatening deterioration.
Agents already covered elsewhere in this app — go there for management

items: Calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers, and clonidine — see Cardiovascular Drug Toxicity for management detail. Note: dihydropyridine CCBs (e.g. nifedipine) and verapamil are the most frequently implicated in symptomatic small-child ingestions; general recommendation is at least 6 hours of observation after a regular-release exposure and 12-24 hours after any sustained/extended-release exposure in a child under 6.
Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) and other psychiatric medications — see Psychiatric Drug Toxicity and the sodium bicarbonate card for QRS-widening management.

Sulfonylureas (glyburide, glipizide, chlorpropamide) — a single tablet can cause delayed, prolonged, and recurrent hypoglycemia in a small child, sometimes many hours after ingestion; see the antidotes/reversal reference for octreotide/dextrose management. Any sulfonylurea exposure in a small child warrants extended glucose monitoring given the delayed and recurrent hypoglycemia risk, not a single normal glucose check and discharge.
Opioids — a single adult-dose opioid tablet or patch can cause respiratory depression in a small child; see the opioid toxicity reference and high-dose naloxone/nalmefene card.

body.text:
Found in some topical liniments/vapor rubs and Campho-Phenique-type products at higher concentrations than commonly assumed. As little as roughly 1 gram (well under two teaspoons of some concentrated products) has caused fatality in a toddler.

Onset is FAST — seizures can occur within 5-90 minutes of ingestion, sometimes with minimal warning symptoms beforehand.

There is no antidote — management is supportive:
- seizure control with benzodiazepines
- airway protection
- close monitoring

Activated charcoal is of limited value given how rapidly camphor is absorbed and how quickly seizures can occur.

Oil of wintergreen and similar concentrated topical liniments/muscle rubs contain methyl salicylate at a concentration far higher than aspirin tablets — under a teaspoon (roughly 4-5 mL) has been fatal in a toddler, an amount that looks trivial to a caregiver.

Treat clinically as a severe salicylate/aspirin overdose (tachypnea, metabolic acidosis with respiratory alkalosis, tinnitus in an older child, altered mental status) but recognize the MUCH smaller volume required to reach a lethal dose compared to swallowed aspirin tablets.

Management follows standard salicylate toxicity principles — alkalinization, correcting volume/electrolyte status, and involving toxicology/nephrology early for possible hemodialysis in severe cases.

A single adult tablet of chloroquine (or related antimalarials) can produce lethal cardiac dysfunction (QRS widening, ventricular dysrhythmia, hypotension) and seizures in a small child — onset can be rapid, sometimes within an hour.

This is one of the more dramatic examples of how a routine adult prescription medication can be catastrophic in toddler-sized doses.

Management is largely supportive and follows sodium-channel-blocker-toxicity principles:
- sodium bicarbonate for QRS widening
- benzodiazepines for seizures
- aggressive hemodynamic support

Involve toxicology/poison control early given how rapidly deterioration can occur and the relative rarity of this specific exposure.
General approach to any suspected one-pill-can-kill exposure

items: Take the history seriously even if the child looks well at presentation — 'found the bottle open, one pill possibly missing' is enough to trigger observation/workup for agents on this list.
Contact poison control early — they can help identify the specific product/concentration involved and give current, product-specific guidance.

Decide observation duration based on the specific agent's expected onset and duration of action (including whether it's an extended-release formulation) rather than a single fixed rule for every ingestion.
Have a low threshold for a monitored bed even in an asymptomatic child, given how fast some of these agents can turn a well-appearing toddler critically ill.
